## A scale hands you seven chords for free

Take degrees 1, 3 and 5 of a major scale and you have its tonic triad. Start on
degree 2 and take every other degree again, and another chord appears without
one note from outside the key. Do that from all seven starting points and the
scale has quietly handed you a family of seven triads. You never chose their
qualities. The scale's uneven spacing chose for you.

These are the *diatonic chords*, and Roman numerals name them by scale position
while encoding quality in the case: uppercase for major, lowercase for minor,
with a marker on the diminished chord at degree 7. So `I, V, vi, IV` stores
relationships and not note names. Bind that sequence to a different key and
every pitch changes while the sequence of harmonic jobs stays recognisable.

## One symbolic plan, four keys

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96
use_synth :piano

define :diatonic_triads do |root|
  notes = scale(root, :major).to_a
  7.times.map do |degree|
    [notes[degree], notes[(degree + 2) % 7], notes[(degree + 4) % 7]].
      each_with_index.map { |pitch, i| pitch + (i > 0 && pitch < notes[degree] ? 12 : 0) }
  end
end

define :render_progression do |root, numerals|
  lookup = {I: 0, ii: 1, iii: 2, IV: 3, V: 4, vi: 5, vii_dim: 6}
  chords = diatonic_triads(root)
  numerals.each do |numeral|
    play_chord chords[lookup[numeral]], release: 1.6
    sleep 2
  end
end

progression = [:I, :V, :vi, :IV]
[:c3, :d3, :e3, :f3].each do |key|
  puts "key #{key}"
  render_progression key, progression
end
```

You get four passes that climb through four keys along one harmonic route. I
sets up home. V raises the expectation of a return. vi takes that expectation
and points it at a related minor chord instead. IV opens a second road back
toward I. Because one symbolic array drives every rendering, the shared shape is
much easier to hear than it would be in four unrelated note lists.

## Bend the plan, then look inside it

1. Swap the progression for `[:I, :IV, :V, :I]`. V now spends its tension on an
   immediate tonic and the last boundary closes harder. Which version would you
   rather loop for two minutes?

2. Print the seven C-major triads as MIDI integers and compare the size of each
   chord's two thirds. You'll get major, minor, minor, major, major, minor,
   diminished. Nothing in the code stores that pattern; it falls out of the
   scale.

3. Arpeggiate each chord inside the renderer. Progression and pitch content stay
   fixed, and the separate attacks show you which alternating scale degrees
   built each harmony.

## Why the numerals earn their place

The scale array holds seven distinct degrees plus a repeated octave. To build a
triad you take every other one. Modular indexing wraps the upper picks back to
the start of the seven-note collection, and the octave correction puts them
above the chord's own root again so the array ascends.

No quality table appears anywhere in the code. The spacing already sitting in
the major scale produces the whole major-minor-minor-major-major-minor-
diminished sequence, which is a nice check on your understanding: if you can
predict all seven qualities from the step formula, you've understood the scale
and not memorised a chart.

Case carries information that a bare degree number would lose. `:V` states a
position and the major quality that position takes in a major key. Later on a
chromatic chord will alter that default, and a symbolic layer gives the
alteration somewhere to live. Collapse everything to zero-based indices too
early and you erase the distinction the notation exists to carry.

Roman numerals also make comparison across keys practical. The dominant of C
major and the dominant of F major share no pitch classes at all, yet both do the
same job and pull toward their own tonic. That's late binding in musical form:
the progression stores intent, and `render_progression` resolves it against
whatever root you hand it. A list of MIDI arrays transposes perfectly well and
still can't tell you why one chord follows another.

The lookup hash also shows the limits of a short symbol. Major `:I` and minor
`:i` need different defaults, and inversion belongs in its own field, not in a
proliferating set of names. A fuller record would carry `:degree`, `:quality`
and `:bass`, leaving the concrete voicing to the renderer. For a diatonic
comparison in one mode, these compact symbols work because their defaults are
unambiguous.

## Test the plan before you voice it

Write `progression_notes(root, numerals)` so that it returns chord arrays
without playing anything, then evaluate `[:vi, :IV, :I, :V]` in all twelve
roots. Every result should hold four three-note chords, and every pitch class
should belong to the matching major key. Those checks are cheap and they run
silently.

Once they pass, pick one key and render it with inversions chosen by [Lesson 27](27-inversions-voicing.qmd)'s
`voice_near`. Print the movement totals beside the root-position version. Your
symbolic plan should survive both the structural test and the voicing search
without a single edit, which is the whole point of keeping it symbolic.
